## First & Corresponding Author

**Green R\***, Richards H, Ozbilek D, Tyrrell F, Barton V, Zhang Z, Lovell SC, Gifford DR, Lagator M, McBain AJ, Krašovec R\*, Knight CG\*. [Antimutator and mutational spectrum effects can combine to reduce evolutionary potential in *Escherichia coli* Δ*nudJ*.]{.underline} **Molecular Biology and Evolution**. 2025

Bacteria with increased mutation rates ('mutators') are common, especially in stressful environments such as infections treated with antibiotics. However, bacteria with lower than average mutation rates ('antimutators') are far rarer. In this study we measured the mutation rates of a set of *E. coli* knockout strains finding that one of these (called Δ*nudJ*) had a mutation rate \>6-fold lower than the wildtype! Not only did this strain mutate less but it also had different types of mutations. This change in its mutation spectra made highly costly resistance mutations more accessible. Therefore, by removing just one gene we can make antibiotic resistance less common (low muatation rate) and more costly (altered mutation spectrum).

I wrote this paper using hundreds of *E. coli* mutation rate assays and sequenced isolates collected by myself, Hugh Richards and my mentee heroes (Tyrrell F & Barton V & Zhang Z). I was really lucky to be able to incorporate 'cost of resistance' data collected by Deniz Ozbilek.

Associated data and code: https://osf.io/mu2ek/

**Green R\***, Bawn M, Angus-Whiteoak A, Jago M, Whelan FJ, Lagator M, Hall N, Knight CG\*, Krašovec R\*. [Identifying rare spontaneous mutations through wildtype E. coli population sequencing.]{.underline} **bioRxiv**. 2025 

This bioinformatic project demonstrates the use of deep, population sequencing as an alternative method for microbial mutation rate estimation. This approach overcomes multiple drawbacks of existing methods for mutation rate estimation by combining the rapid, liquid-based features of fluctuation assays with the genome-wide nature of mutation accumulation assays.

Associated data and code: https://osf.io/gztjk/

## First Author

**Green R**, Wang H, Botchey C, Zhang SN, Wadsworth C, Tyrrell F, Letton J, McBain AJ, Paszek P, Krašovec R\*, Knight CG\*. Collective peroxide detoxification determines microbial mutation rate plasticity in E. coli. **Plos Biology**. 2024

This study demonstrates the mechanism responsible for the inverse relationship between mutation rates and population density in observed in many microbial species. Using **dynamical computational modelling** and **in culture mutation rate estimation**, we show that the negative relationship between mutation rate and population density arises from the collective ability of microbial populations to control concentrations of hydrogen peroxide. Together, these model-guided experiments provide a mechanistic explanation for density associated mutation rate plasticity, applicable across all domains of life, and frame mutation rate as a dynamic trait shaped by microbial community composition.

Associated code and data at the publisher’s website

## Projects in the works...

- How do bacterial species impact one another's mutation rates in mixed-species co-culture? What are the knock-on effects of this for evolutionary rescue when faced with antibiotic selection?

- How common are defective viral genomes in avian and seasonal influenza? How do these associate with host identity?

- How do the positions and density of mutational hotspots for defective viral genome generation evolve over time? Does this place constraints on the evolving influenza genome?
